notes.meaning: The Roman emperor ordered a census so that every person across the empire could be counted for taxes. God used this powerful ruler's decree to bring Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem, just as the ancient prophets had foretold. Even great world leaders unknowingly serve God's greater plan.
Luke explains that this registration took place while Quirinius was governing Syria. God made sure the right rulers were in place so that the promise about the Messiah's birthplace would come true.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Secular records date Quirinius's official term to around A.D. 6, so some scholars believe Quirinius held an earlier military post or joint administrative role in the region during this first count.

notes.meaning: People had to travel back to the town where their ancestors came from in order to register. Even though moving whole families was difficult, people obeyed the emperor's order.

Joseph made the long, uphill journey south from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem in Judea. He traveled there because Bethlehem was the historic hometown of King David, and Joseph was David's descendant.

Joseph went to register along with Mary, who was promised to him in marriage and was soon going to have her baby. Taking Mary with him protected her and ensured that her child was born in David's town.
While Joseph and Mary were staying in Bethlehem, the time arrived for her baby to be born. God guided their steps so that the birth happened in the exact place promised by scripture.

Mary gave birth to her firstborn Son, wrapped Him tightly in strips of cloth, and placed Him in a feeding trough for animals. There was no guest room available for them, so the Savior of the world began His earthly life in a humble shelter.

differ.view: The word firstborn indicates that Mary and Joseph went on to have other children together after Jesus was born.
The title firstborn refers to the legal status of the first male child under Jewish law and does not prove whether later siblings were born.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Mary remained a virgin throughout her entire life, and calling Jesus her firstborn simply reflects the biblical legal phrase for the child who opened the womb.

notes.meaning: Shepherds were out in the fields near Bethlehem, taking turns watching their sheep through the dark hours of the night. God chose these humble, hardworking men to be the very first people to hear about the Savior's birth.
An angel suddenly appeared beside the shepherds, and the brilliant light of God's presence shone all around them. The shepherds were terrified by this sudden display of heavenly splendor.

The angel told the frightened shepherds not to be afraid, because he was bringing wonderful news. This message was filled with great joy and was meant first for Israel and ultimately for the entire world.
The angel announced that a Savior was born that very night in Bethlehem, the city of David. This child was the Christ, God's chosen King, who had come to rescue humanity from sin.

The angel gave the shepherds a surprising sign to help them identify the right baby. Instead of resting in a royal crib, the infant King would be wrapped in cloth strips and lying in an animal feeding trough.
A vast army of heavenly angels suddenly joined the first angel to praise God together. The whole host of heaven celebrated because God's great work of salvation had finally arrived on earth.
The angels sang praise to God in highest heaven and declared peace on earth to the people who receive His grace. Jesus came to bring true peace and reconciliation between God and humanity.

differ.view: God's good will and offered peace extend freely to all people everywhere who are willing to turn to Him.
God's special favor and saving peace are granted specifically to His chosen people according to His sovereign grace.

notes.meaning: As soon as the angels went back up into heaven, the shepherds urged each other to hurry to Bethlehem. They had full faith in God's message and wanted to see what the Lord had revealed to them.
The shepherds ran quickly into town and found Mary, Joseph, and the newborn baby lying in the feeding trough. Seeing everything match the angel's description filled them with wonder and joy.
After the shepherds saw the baby, they immediately told everyone what the angel had spoken concerning Him. These humble workers became the very first messengers to spread the good news about Jesus.
Everyone who heard the shepherds' story was astonished by what they reported. The listeners marveled that the long-awaited King had arrived in such poor and lowly circumstances.
Mary carefully held on to all these words and events, thinking deeply about them in her heart. She quietly reflected on how God was fulfilling every promise He had made about her Son.

The shepherds went back to their fields, praising and glorifying God for everything they had experienced. Their hearts overflowed with worship because every detail matched what the angel had told them.
When the baby was eight days old, He was circumcised according to God's covenant with Abraham and given the name Jesus. This was the exact name the angel had announced before Mary even conceived Him.

After the forty days of ritual cleansing required by the law of Moses, Mary and Joseph brought Jesus to the temple in Jerusalem. They came to dedicate the child to the Lord in complete obedience to God's commands.

differ.view: The purification offering shows that Mary was a normal, sinful human being who needed ritual cleansing just like every other mother under the law.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Mary remained completely sinless throughout her life and submitted to the law out of humble obedience and love for God rather than from personal moral guilt.

notes.meaning: The law taught that every firstborn male child belonged in a special way to the Lord. God established this rule to remind His people how He had spared their firstborn sons during the Passover in Egypt.

Joseph and Mary offered a pair of small birds as their sacrifice at the temple. God's law allowed poor families who could not afford a lamb to bring doves or pigeons instead, showing that Jesus grew up in a very modest home.

An upright and devout man named Simeon lived in Jerusalem, patiently waiting for God to comfort and rescue Israel. The Holy Spirit was resting upon him, giving him a strong hope for the coming Messiah.

The Holy Spirit had revealed to Simeon that he would not die before he had seen the Lord's promised Messiah. Simeon trusted this promise and waited faithfully to see God's salvation with his own eyes.
